prompt: A lessee signs a 5-year lease for equipment. The present value of the lease payments is 100,000. Record the lease at commencement under IFRS 16.

reasoning: IFRS 16 puts almost every lease on the balance sheet.
Liability = PV of payments; ROU asset = liability + direct costs + prepayments − incentives.

why_it_matters: Leases are debt in substance; since 2019 they show up in net debt and EBITDA.
common_trap: Expensing the payments as rent with nothing on the balance sheet.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IFRS 16: single lessee model — every lease is a finance-style lease (except short-term/low-value exemptions).
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 842: lessee classifies finance vs operating; both go on the balance sheet, but an operating lease has one straight-line lease cost.

prompt: The lease liability is 100,000 at an 8% rate. At the end of year 1 the lessee pays 25,000. Record the payment including interest.

reasoning: The rest (17,000) reduces the liability.

why_it_matters: Under IFRS 16 the principal part moves to financing cash flows, so CFO and EBITDA rise versus the old rent model.
common_trap: Charging the full payment to the liability or to expense.

prompt: The right-of-use asset of 100,000 is depreciated straight-line over the 5-year lease term. Record year 1 depreciation.

reasoning: Depreciate over the shorter of lease term and useful life (unless ownership transfers).

why_it_matters: Depreciation + interest is front-loaded compared with flat rent, so early-year profit is lower.
common_trap: Using the asset's full economic life when the lease is shorter.

prompt: A company rents a storage unit for 6 months and elects the short-term lease exemption. It pays this month's 3,000. Record it.

reasoning: Leases of 12 months or less (and low-value assets under IFRS) may be expensed straight-line.

why_it_matters: Heavy use of short-term leases keeps commitments off the balance sheet; read the note.
common_trap: Capitalising a lease that qualifies for the exemption (allowed, but not required).

prompt: The lessee pays 2,000 of legal fees that would not have been incurred without the lease (initial direct costs). Record them.

reasoning: Initial direct costs are added to the ROU asset and depreciated, not expensed.

why_it_matters: Small detail, but it shows how the ROU asset can differ from the lease liability.
common_trap: Adding direct costs to the lease liability.

prompt: A manufacturer leases a machine it made (cost 80,000) under a finance lease. The PV of lease payments (and fair value) is 100,000. Record the lease at commencement as lessor.

reasoning: Manufacturer/dealer lessors recognise selling profit at commencement.
The asset is replaced by a lease receivable; interest income follows.

why_it_matters: Equipment makers can boost sales with leasing; check receivable quality and residual risk.
common_trap: Keeping the machine in PP&E and recording rental income.

prompt: The lessor's lease receivable is 100,000 at 8%. It receives the year-end payment of 25,000. Record the receipt.

reasoning: Interest = 100,000 × 8% = 8,000; the rest reduces the receivable.

why_it_matters: The mirror image of the lessee: interest income declines as the receivable falls.
common_trap: Recognising the whole receipt as revenue.

prompt: Which indicates that a lessor should classify a lease as a finance (sales-type) lease?
options: The lease term covers the major part of the asset's economic life
The lease is cancellable at any time without penalty

reasoning: Indicators: ownership transfer, bargain purchase option, major part of life, PV ≈ substantially all fair value, specialised asset.
If substantially all risks and rewards transfer, it is a finance lease.

why_it_matters: Lessor classification decides whether profit is recognised upfront or rent is recognised over time.
common_trap: Thinking IFRS 16 removed lessor classification (it did not).

prompt: Annual lease payments of 10,000 in arrears for 3 years, discount rate 10%. Initial lease liability (to the nearest unit)?

reasoning: Annuity factor (3 yrs, 10%) ≈ 2.487

why_it_matters: Lease liabilities are present values; a higher discount rate lowers reported debt.
common_trap: Recording the undiscounted 30,000.

prompt: Which discount rate does a lessee use to measure the lease liability?
options: The rate implicit in the lease if readily determinable, otherwise the lessee's incremental borrowing rate

reasoning: In practice most lessees use their incremental borrowing rate.

why_it_matters: Rate choice directly changes the liability and the split between interest and depreciation.
common_trap: Using a group-wide rate for leases of very different terms.

prompt: A retailer moves from expensing rent to IFRS 16. What happens to EBITDA and net debt?

reasoning: Rent leaves EBITDA; depreciation and interest replace it below EBITDA.
Lease liabilities join net debt.

why_it_matters: Net debt/EBITDA can look similar but EV/EBITDA must include lease liabilities in EV for consistency.
common_trap: Using post-IFRS 16 EBITDA with pre-IFRS 16 EV (missing leases).

prompt: Compared with a flat rent expense, how does total IFRS 16 lease cost (interest + depreciation) behave over a lease?
options: Higher in early years, lower later (front-loaded)

reasoning: Interest is highest when the liability is largest.
Depreciation is straight-line.

why_it_matters: Companies with young lease portfolios show lower profit than under rent accounting.
common_trap: Assuming total expense is unchanged each year.

prompt: Under US GAAP ASC 842, how does a lessee present an operating lease in the income statement?
options: A single straight-line lease cost in operating expenses (ROU asset and liability are still on the balance sheet)
Off balance sheet with rent expense

reasoning: ASC 842 keeps the operating-lease income statement pattern but puts the lease on the balance sheet.

why_it_matters: US and IFRS EBITDA are not comparable for lease-heavy companies (retail, airlines).
common_trap: Comparing EBITDA of a US and an IFRS retailer without adjustment.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: Interest and depreciation for all leases (EBITDA excludes lease cost).
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: Operating leases: single lease cost inside EBITDA; finance leases: interest + amortisation.

prompt: What does a lessee include in the lease liability for a residual value guarantee?
options: The amount it expects to pay under the guarantee

reasoning: Lessees include amounts expected to be payable under residual value guarantees.
Lessors include the guaranteed and unguaranteed residual in their net investment.

why_it_matters: Guarantees shift asset-value risk to the lessee; they are contingent debt.
common_trap: Ignoring guarantees in leverage.

prompt: A 5-year shop lease has an option to extend for 5 more years. The shop has expensive fit-outs and is a top performer. What lease term is used?
options: 10 years, if extension is reasonably certain given economic incentives

reasoning: Include optional periods when exercise is reasonably certain (fit-outs, location importance).

why_it_matters: Lease-term judgements can double the reported liability.
common_trap: Using only the non-cancellable period.

prompt: Lease (IFRS 16 definition)

answer.meaning: A contract that conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration.
answer.formula: Identified asset + right to obtain substantially all economic benefits + right to direct the use
answer.interpretation: If the supplier can substitute the asset freely, there is no lease (it is a service).
answer.high_signals: Embedded leases in supply or outsourcing contracts.

why_it_matters: Structuring a contract as a 'service' keeps it off the balance sheet.
common_trap: Only looking at contracts labelled 'lease'.

prompt: A company sells its head office to an investor (a valid sale under IFRS 15) and leases it back for 10 years. How much gain can it recognise?
options: Only the gain relating to the rights transferred to the buyer; the part relating to the retained right of use is not recognised
The gain spread equally over 10 years

reasoning: The seller-lessee measures the ROU asset as the retained portion of the old carrying amount.
If the transfer is not a sale, it is a financing.

why_it_matters: Sale-leasebacks raise cash but add lease debt; profit is limited.
common_trap: Booking the full gain as if the building were gone.

prompt: How does a lessor account for an operating lease of a building?
options: Keeps the building on its balance sheet, depreciates it and recognises rental income (usually straight-line)
Derecognises the building and records a receivable
Records sales revenue for the building

reasoning: Risks and rewards stay with the lessor.

why_it_matters: Real-estate companies earn rent and keep asset risk.
common_trap: Mixing up lessor operating and finance lease models.

prompt: A shop lease charges 5% of sales instead of fixed rent. How is this treated?
options: Payments linked to sales are expensed as incurred, not included in the lease liability
Included in the liability at expected sales

reasoning: Only payments that depend on an index or rate (or are in-substance fixed) go into the liability.

why_it_matters: Turnover-based rents keep leases off-balance-sheet and appear in EBITDA.
common_trap: Comparing retailers' lease debt without checking variable-rent structures.

prompt: Lease liability at the start of year 2 is 83,000 at 8%. Interest expense for year 2?
why_it_matters: Interest falls each year as the liability amortises.
common_trap: Using the original liability every year.

prompt: Under IFRS 16, where are the principal portions of lease payments shown in the cash flow statement?

reasoning: Principal: financing. Interest: per the entity's IAS 7 policy. Short-term/variable payments: operating.

why_it_matters: FCF definitions must subtract lease payments, or retailers look far more cash-generative than they are.
common_trap: Ignoring lease payments in FCF.

prompt: You compare two retailers: one owns its stores, the other leases them all. How do you make their EBITDA, leverage and FCF comparable?

answer.model_answer: For the leaser under IFRS 16: EBITDA excludes rent, so include lease liabilities in net debt and EV (EV/EBITDA consistent). For FCF, subtract lease payments (principal + interest) to get FCF after leases, comparable with the owner's FCF after capex. Alternatively use EBITDAR-style metrics or pre-IFRS 16 (rent-adjusted) EBITDA with leases excluded from debt — but be consistent on both numerator and denominator. Also compare ROIC with ROU assets in invested capital, and check lease terms, variable rents and short-term exemptions that leave commitments off the balance sheet.

reasoning: Align each metric's numerator and denominator.

why_it_matters: Lease-heavy vs asset-owning comparisons are a staple of retail and airline analysis.
common_trap: Mixing post-IFRS 16 EBITDA with EV that excludes lease debt.
